stimuli.title: Two maps of college attainment, described in words (hypothetical data)
stimuli.text:
**Map 1** shows the share of adults with a college degree in each of a country's six provinces. All six provinces fall between 28 and 34 percent, so the map is shaded in a single color.

**Map 2** shows the same measure for the 140 districts of one of those provinces, Province E, each district shaded by its value. District values range from 9 to 61 percent. The highest values cluster around the provincial capital and along a rail corridor that runs south from it; the lowest are in the mountain districts of the north.

stimuli.title: Three world maps, described in words
stimuli.text:
**Map 1:** Lines of latitude and longitude are straight and cross at right angles. Greenland looks about as large as Africa, although Africa is about 14 times larger in area.

**Map 2:** Greenland and Africa are drawn in correct proportion to their areas, but Africa and South America look stretched from north to south and squeezed from east to west.

**Map 3:** The lines of longitude curve toward the poles. No property is shown exactly; shape, area, distance and direction are all slightly distorted, with the worst distortion near the poles.

stimuli.title: Population pyramid of Country M, described in words (hypothetical data)
stimuli.text: Each bar from ages 0-4 up to 15-19 is narrower than the bar just above it, so the base of the pyramid is narrower than its middle. The widest bars are the age groups from 45-49 to 60-64. From age 70 upward, the bars for women are clearly wider than the bars for men. Country M's total population fell slightly over the last five years, even though more people moved into the country than left it.

stimuli.title: A city street, described in words (practice description)
stimuli.text: On one street in a large North American city, shop signs are written in English and Vietnamese. A Buddhist temple stands two doors from a church whose noticeboard lists services in both languages. Restaurants serve pho and burgers on the same menu, and a supermarket stocks produce imported from Southeast Asia. Older residents say the street was mostly Italian American in the 1950s; a few Italian bakeries and the building of a former Catholic school still stand.

stimuli.title: The spread of a new sport in one country, described as a series of maps (hypothetical)
stimuli.text:
**2005:** The first professional teams appear in the country's three largest cities.

**2012:** Teams have been founded in the next ten largest cities, which are scattered across the country, but in almost no smaller places.

**2020:** Amateur leagues have appeared in many small towns, usually first in the towns closest to a city that has a team, and then in the towns next to those.

stimuli.title: A pilgrimage town, described in words (practice description)
stimuli.text: Stone steps lead down to a broad river, where pilgrims bathe at dawn and set small oil lamps on the water. Cremation grounds lie at the river's edge. The lanes behind are lined with shrines and with shops selling flowers, incense and images of gods. During the main festival the town's population rises several times over, and the government sets up tent camps, clinics and extra trains.

stimuli.title: Election results in State W's five legislative districts (hypothetical data)
stimuli.text:

| 2 | 85,000 | 15,000 |
| 3 | 38,000 | 62,000 |
| 4 | 41,000 | 59,000 |
| 5 | 46,000 | 54,000 |

stimuli.title: Map of Country V, described in words (hypothetical)
stimuli.text: Country V is long and narrow, stretching about ten times farther from north to south than from east to west. Its capital lies on a central plain where most people speak the national language and share the majority religion. The mountainous far north is home to an ethnic group with its own language and religion; that region elects its own assembly, which runs its schools and police. Railways run from the capital to every region except the north, which is reached by a single highway through a mountain pass.

stimuli.title: Three international borders, described in words (hypothetical)
stimuli.text:
**Border 1** follows the crest of a high mountain range that separated two farming peoples long before either state existed.

**Border 2** is a straight line of longitude that two colonial powers agreed on in the 1800s. It crosses a dry grassland and divides the seasonal pastures of one herding people.

**Border 3** winds between villages so that each village lies in the state whose language its people speak. It was drawn after a war in the 1900s, in an area that had long been settled.

stimuli.title: Rural land use around a market town, described in words (hypothetical)
stimuli.text:
A market town stands alone on a flat, uniform plain, and all farm goods are carried to it by cart. Around it lie four rings of land use.

**Ring 1**, nearest the town: dairy farms and market gardens growing vegetables and fruit.

**Ring 2:** woodland cut for firewood and building timber.

**Ring 3:** fields of wheat and other grains.

**Ring 4**, farthest out: cattle and sheep grazing. Beyond Ring 4 the land is not used.

stimuli.title: A hillside farming landscape in a humid tropical region, described in words (practice description)
stimuli.text: The slopes are cut into narrow, stepped fields held up by low walls of earth and stone. Water runs from the highest field to the lowest through small channels, and families plant rice seedlings by hand in the flooded fields. Houses stand close together in a village at the foot of the slope, with small vegetable plots between them, and a few water buffalo graze along the paths.

stimuli.title: A large city, described in words (practice description)
stimuli.text: An old central plaza holds the cathedral, government offices and the main business district. A wide, tree-lined avenue runs out from the center with offices, shops, parks and upscale apartment towers along it, ending at a newer business district near the edge of the city. Middle-income neighborhoods form rings farther out; their houses, first built simply, have been enlarged and improved by the owners over many years. On the edge of the city, on steep hillsides and along a polluted river, lie self-built settlements without full water or sewer service.

stimuli.title: A new industrial district, described in words (practice description)
stimuli.text: A government sets aside a coastal district beside a deepwater port. Foreign companies that build factories there pay lower taxes and bring in parts without paying tariffs, as long as they export what they make. Within ten years the district holds electronics and clothing factories that employ mostly young women from inland provinces, and the fishing villages around it have grown into a city.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by comparing the two maps?
options: The rail corridor lowers attainment near it
Education levels are even across Province E
Mountain districts have the most graduates
National data can hide large local differences
Province-level data are more precise than district data
questions.explanation: Map 1 makes the provinces look alike, but Map 2 shows a range of 9 to 61 percent inside one of them. Changing the scale of analysis reveals variation that the larger units average away.

questions.stem: Map 2 is best described as which kind of map?
questions.explanation: Map 2 shades each district by a rate, which is a choropleth map. An isoline map joins points of equal value with lines, and a cartogram resizes the districts themselves.

questions.stem: The high values around the capital and along the rail corridor are best explained by
options: lower population density near the provincial capital
mountains in the north that block migration to the capital
colleges and skilled jobs clustered along transport links
forced resettlement of graduates from the north
a larger share of farmland along the rail line
questions.explanation: Universities and jobs that need degrees concentrate in the capital and in places well connected to it, so graduates live there. The mountain districts are less accessible and have fewer such jobs.

questions.stem: A ship's navigator would choose a Mercator projection mainly because it
options: shows lines of constant compass bearing as straight
keeps every distance from the map's center true
shows the true area of land at high latitudes
draws each pole as a single point without stretching
splits the oceans to reduce distortion of land
questions.explanation: On a Mercator projection a line of constant compass direction is straight, which made it the standard sea chart. The price is a huge enlargement of area toward the poles.

questions.stem: The delivery area of a city's daily newspaper, centered on its printing plant, is best described as
questions.explanation: A functional (nodal) region is organized around a central point and the links to it, here the plant and its delivery routes. A formal region shares one trait throughout, such as a language.

questions.stem: A clinic finds that most of its patients live within 5 km and very few come from 30 km away. This pattern illustrates
questions.explanation: Distance decay is the drop in interaction as distance grows. Time-space compression is the opposite tendency, as technology makes distant places feel closer.

questions.stem: What is the rate of natural increase of Country B?
questions.explanation: The rate of natural increase is the crude birth rate minus the crude death rate, as a percent: (33 - 7) / 1,000 = 2.6%. Adding the two rates gives 4.0%, and 26 is the gap per 1,000, not per 100.

questions.stem: Which country is most likely in stage 5 of the demographic transition model?
questions.explanation: Stage 5 is natural decrease: Country D's death rate (11) is above its birth rate (9). Country E has low rates that still give slight growth, which is stage 4.

questions.stem: Country A's high total fertility rate is most likely linked to
options: a high share of women finishing university degrees
low female education and a need for farm labor
questions.explanation: Where few girls stay in school and families farm by hand, children add labor and many are born; Country A's high infant mortality adds to that. The other options describe places with low fertility.

questions.stem: According to Ravenstein's laws of migration, most migrants
questions.explanation: Ravenstein found that most migration is over short distances, that long-distance migrants tend to head for large cities, and that every flow creates a counterflow.

questions.stem: For a farmer who leaves home after years of drought, the drought is
questions.explanation: A push factor drives people out of their origin, and drought is an environmental one. An intervening obstacle lies along the route, not at home.

questions.stem: In the later stages of the epidemiological transition, the leading causes of death become
questions.explanation: As sanitation, vaccines and medicine cut infectious disease, more people live long enough to die of heart disease, cancer and other chronic conditions of old age.

questions.stem: Thomas Malthus argued that population would outgrow the food supply because
options: population grows geometrically and food arithmetically
migration spreads people evenly over the land
food grows geometrically and population arithmetically
birth rates fall as people move to cities
new technology always raises crop yields
questions.explanation: Malthus held that population can double again and again while food output rises only by steady additions, so famine, disease or war would check growth. He did not foresee the gains in farm output.

questions.stem: A country has 26 million people aged 0 to 14, 50 million aged 15 to 64 and 9 million aged 65 and over. What is its dependency ratio?
questions.explanation: The dependency ratio is dependents (under 15 and 65 and over) per 100 people of working age: (26 + 9) / 50 x 100 = 70. Using only the young gives 52, only the old 18.

questions.stem: A government that offers free contraception and rewards couples who have fewer children follows
questions.explanation: Antinatalist policies aim to lower the birth rate. Pronatalist policies, such as child allowances, try to raise it.

questions.stem: The street described is best identified as
questions.explanation: An ethnic enclave is a neighborhood where one ethnic group clusters, with its own shops, worship and language on the signs. The street has none of the office towers of a CBD.

questions.stem: The surviving Italian bakeries and school building illustrate
questions.explanation: Sequent occupance is the layering of the marks that successive groups leave on one place. The Italian American layer remains under the Vietnamese one.

questions.stem: Restaurants that serve pho and burgers on one menu are an example of
questions.explanation: Syncretism blends traits from different cultures into something new. Assimilation would mean the immigrant food giving way to the host culture's entirely.

questions.stem: A rumor that spreads from neighbor to neighbor until most of a town has heard it shows
questions.explanation: Contagious diffusion spreads outward through direct contact, reaching nearby people first, regardless of rank or status.

questions.stem: The spread of a language to a new continent by the migrants who carry it there is
questions.explanation: In relocation diffusion the trait moves with people who leave the hearth. In expansion diffusion (contagious, hierarchical and stimulus) it spreads while staying strong at home.

questions.stem: A fast-food chain sells vegetarian burgers in India, where many people avoid beef. The idea of the burger has spread by
questions.explanation: In stimulus diffusion the underlying idea spreads but is changed to fit the local culture, here a burger without beef.

questions.stem: Which of these religions is an ethnic religion?
questions.explanation: Hinduism is closely tied to the people and landscapes of South Asia and does not seek converts. Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and Sikhism are universalizing religions.

questions.stem: A language that people with different native languages use to trade with one another is
questions.explanation: A lingua franca is a shared second language for trade or diplomacy, such as Swahili in much of East Africa. A creole is a mixed language that has become people's first language.

questions.stem: English and Hindi both belong to which language family?
questions.explanation: Both descend from a common ancestor of the Indo-European family, English in its Germanic branch and Hindi in its Indo-Iranian branch.

questions.stem: What share of the total vote in State W did Party X win?
questions.explanation: Party X won 88,000 + 85,000 + 38,000 + 41,000 + 46,000 = 298,000 of 500,000 votes, or 59.6%. It won only 2 of 5 seats, which is 40% of the seats.

questions.stem: The lopsided results in Districts 1 and 2 show which redistricting technique?
questions.explanation: Packing crowds one party's voters into a few districts it wins by huge margins, wasting votes. Cracking spreads them thinly across many districts.

questions.stem: Taken as a whole, the results are best explained by
questions.explanation: Party Y won 3 of 5 seats with about 40% of the vote because Party X's voters were packed into two districts. Every district casts the same number of votes, so unequal population is not the cause.

questions.stem: A state whose people largely share one ethnic identity and language, such as Iceland, is
questions.explanation: A nation-state is a state whose territory matches that of one nation. A multinational state contains several.

questions.stem: The Kurds, a people spread across several states without a state of their own, are
questions.explanation: A stateless nation is a people with a shared identity and homeland but no sovereign state. Kurds live mainly in Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria.

questions.stem: A boundary drawn across an area before it was densely settled is
questions.explanation: Antecedent boundaries come before most settlement, so the cultural landscape grows up around them. Subsequent boundaries are drawn after settlement.

questions.stem: The European Union, whose member states share some laws and a single market, is
questions.explanation: A supranational organization joins three or more states that give up some sovereignty for shared goals. Its members remain separate sovereign states.

questions.stem: Which is most likely a centrifugal force for a state?
options: A road network reaching every region
A regional language group seeking autonomy
A national team that unites fans
questions.explanation: Centrifugal forces pull a state apart, and a regional group seeking autonomy is one. The other options are centripetal, binding the state together.

questions.stem: A state that divides power between a central government and regional governments, each with powers of its own, has
questions.explanation: In a federal system, such as those of the United States, India or Germany, regional units hold powers the center cannot simply take away. A unitary system concentrates power at the center.

questions.stem: The pattern described matches which model?
questions.explanation: Von Thunen modeled rings of farm land use around a single market on a uniform plain, set by transport cost. Burgess's rings describe land use inside a city.

questions.stem: Dairying and market gardening lie closest to the town mainly because their products
options: need the largest areas of land
need wood from the forest ring nearby
spoil quickly and are costly to carry far
are sold mainly to other countries
grow best in poor, dry soils
questions.explanation: Milk, vegetables and fruit are perishable and bulky for their value, so they pay the high rent near the market to keep transport short. Ranching, which needs the most land, is farthest out.

questions.stem: Today, refrigerated trucks and air freight most directly
options: move grain farming next to towns
raise the cost of shipping fresh food
make the rings described even sharper
weaken distance's effect on land use
questions.explanation: Fast refrigerated transport lets perishable food travel across continents, so global markets, not distance to one town, shape what farmers grow. The model's assumptions fit less well today.

questions.stem: The Fertile Crescent of Southwest Asia is best known as
options: the center of the Green Revolution
the first region of plantation farming
an early hearth of plant domestication
the origin of the potato and maize
questions.explanation: Wheat, barley and lentils were among the crops first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent, one of several independent hearths of the First Agricultural Revolution.

questions.stem: A major criticism of the Green Revolution is that it
options: relied on costly fertilizer, irrigation and seed
ended the use of chemical pesticides
lowered wheat and rice yields in Asia
was adopted mainly by the poorest, landless farmers
questions.explanation: High-yield varieties raised output but needed purchased inputs and water, so better-off farmers gained most, and heavy use of chemicals and groundwater harmed soils and aquifers.

questions.stem: Shifting cultivation is practiced mainly in
options: crowded, irrigated river deltas of East Asia
humid tropical forests with poor soils
questions.explanation: Heavy tropical rain leaches nutrients from forest soils, so farmers burn a plot for its ash, farm it a few years and move on while the forest regrows. Crowded deltas are farmed intensively every year.

questions.stem: Herders who move their animals up to mountain pastures in summer and down to valleys in winter practice
questions.explanation: Transhumance is a seasonal move between fixed pastures. Pastoral nomads move continually with their herds across dry lands, without a fixed home.

questions.stem: A company that owns the farms, the processing plants and the stores that sell its food shows
questions.explanation: Vertical integration is control of several stages of one supply chain. Horizontal integration is buying up competitors at the same stage.

questions.stem: A national survey that divides land into a grid of one-mile squares creates which pattern?
questions.explanation: The township and range system, used across much of the US interior, laid out square sections that still show in fields and roads. Metes and bounds follows natural features.

questions.stem: Under the rank-size rule, about how large would City C be expected to be?
questions.explanation: The rank-size rule says the city of rank n has 1/n the population of the largest city: 12.4 million / 3 is about 4.1 million. Dividing by 2 gives the expected size of City B, 6.2 million.

questions.stem: City A is best described as
questions.explanation: A primate city is more than twice the size of the next largest and dominates its country. City A is over six times the size of City B.

questions.stem: A pattern like Country N's is most common in countries that
options: concentrate political and economic power in one city
have many evenly sized regional centers
have recently moved their capital to a small inland town
are large federations with strong regions
questions.explanation: Primacy develops where government, trade and investment focus on one city, often a former colonial capital or port. Federations with strong regional centers tend toward the rank-size pattern.

questions.stem: In the Burgess concentric zone model, the ring just outside the central business district is
questions.explanation: Burgess placed a zone in transition, with factories and poor, crowded housing, next to the CBD, then workers' homes, better residences and a commuters' zone.

questions.stem: In central place theory, the minimum number of people needed to support a good or service is its
questions.explanation: The threshold is the smallest market that keeps a business going. The range is the maximum distance people will travel for it.

questions.stem: A cluster of offices, malls and housing that grows near a highway interchange on the urban fringe is
questions.explanation: Edge cities grew around the outer beltways of North American metropolitan areas as jobs followed people to the suburbs.

questions.stem: Middle-class newcomers renovating homes in an older inner-city neighborhood, pushing up rents, is
questions.explanation: Gentrification upgrades housing and attracts new businesses but can displace long-time, lower-income residents. Filtering is the reverse, as housing passes down to poorer households.

questions.stem: Walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods with homes close to shops and transit are goals of
questions.explanation: New urbanism designs compact neighborhoods where daily needs are a short walk away, in contrast to car-dependent sprawl.

questions.stem: Bid-rent theory helps explain why
options: every location in a city costs the same
land costs most near the city center
farms are found next to the CBD
cities grow in wedges along rail lines
questions.explanation: Businesses bid most for the accessible land at the center, so rents and densities are highest there and fall with distance. Wedges along routes are Hoyt's sector model.

questions.stem: By how many percentage points did the secondary sector's share fall from 1995 to 2020?
questions.explanation: The secondary share fell from 31% to 18%, a drop of 13 points. Measuring from 1970 (34%) gives 16, and 23 is the rise in the tertiary share.

questions.stem: The change in Country T's secondary sector from 1995 to 2020 is best described as
questions.explanation: Deindustrialization is the decline of manufacturing's share of jobs as a country shifts to services. Industrialization would raise the secondary share.

questions.stem: Which global process most likely contributed to the fall in Country T's secondary sector?
options: New tariffs that kept out goods made in other countries
Rapid population growth in rural areas
Factories moving to countries with lower wages
A fall in the number of service jobs
A rise in the share of farm workers
questions.explanation: As transport and communication costs fell, many firms moved manufacturing to countries with cheaper labor, a new international division of labor, while services grew at home.

questions.stem: In Rostow's stages of economic growth, the stage in which a few leading industries drive rapid growth is
questions.explanation: Rostow's take-off stage sees a few manufacturing industries grow fast and investment rise. The drive to maturity spreads technology across the whole economy.

questions.stem: In Wallerstein's world-systems theory, countries that mainly supply raw materials and low-wage labor to wealthier ones are the
questions.explanation: The periphery exports raw materials and low-value goods to the core, which keeps the high-value, high-profit activities.

questions.stem: Under Weber's least cost theory, a copper smelter that removes most of the weight of the ore is best located
questions.explanation: A bulk-reducing industry locates near its raw material, because shipping the lighter finished metal costs less than shipping the heavy ore.

questions.stem: Besides reproductive health and political empowerment, the Gender Inequality Index measures
questions.explanation: The UN's Gender Inequality Index combines reproductive health, empowerment (seats in parliament and secondary education) and labor force participation. Income per person is part of the Human Development Index.

questions.stem: A country with high income per person but short life expectancy and little schooling would most likely rank
options: outside the HDI, which counts only income
near the top of the Gender Inequality Index
lower on the HDI than on income alone
the same on the HDI as on income alone
higher on the HDI than on income alone
questions.explanation: The HDI combines income per person with life expectancy and years of schooling, so weak health and education pull a rich country's HDI rank below its income rank, as in some oil exporters.

questions.stem: Small loans to people, often women, who cannot borrow from ordinary banks are called
questions.explanation: Microloans help people start or grow small businesses. Structural adjustment loans are large loans to governments with policy conditions.

questions.stem: What is the physiological density of Country S?
questions.explanation: Physiological density is people per unit of arable land. Country S has 81 million people and 30% of 450,000 sq km, or 135,000 sq km, of arable land: 81,000,000 / 135,000 = 600. The value 180 is its arithmetic density.

questions.stem: Which country's farmland has to support the most people per square kilometer?
questions.explanation: Country P's physiological density is 48 million / 60,000 sq km of arable land = 800, the highest. Country T has the highest arithmetic density (250), but half its land is arable, so its physiological density is only 500.

questions.stem: Country R's arithmetic density is low, yet its physiological density is many times higher. The most likely reason is that
options: most of its farms grow crops for export
its census undercounts people in cities
its population is growing very fast
very little of its land can be farmed
most of its people live in rural villages
questions.explanation: Country R has 12 people per sq km overall but 400 per sq km of arable land, because only 3% of its land is arable, as in a country of desert, ice or mountains. Rural living or fast growth would not create that gap.

questions.stem: Collecting data about Earth's surface from satellites or aircraft, without direct contact, is called
questions.explanation: Remote sensing gathers images and readings from a distance. A GIS layers and analyzes data that may come from remote sensing, and GPS fixes a location.

questions.stem: The view that the environment sets limits but people choose how to use it is called
questions.explanation: Possibilism holds that nature offers a range of options and culture decides among them. Environmental determinism, which it replaced, claimed that the environment dictates how societies develop.

questions.stem: Overnight shipping and video calls have made faraway places feel much closer. Geographers call this
questions.explanation: Time-space compression is the shrinking of the time and effort needed to connect places, driven by transport and communication technology. Distance decay describes interaction falling with distance.

questions.stem: The narrow base of Country M's pyramid most likely reflects
options: high birth rates in rural areas
a fertility rate below replacement level
a large inflow of young migrant families
questions.explanation: When each younger age group is smaller than the one before it, fewer children are being born than in the past, the mark of fertility below about 2.1. A baby boom would widen the base.

questions.stem: The wider bars for women at ages 70 and over are best explained by
options: older men moving into the country
questions.explanation: Women outlive men in almost every country, so the oldest age groups have more women. More boys than girls are born, not fewer.

questions.stem: Which policy would Country M's government be most likely to adopt?
options: Limits on the number of children per family
A lower retirement age for all workers
Paid parental leave and child allowances
Closing the border to all immigrants
questions.explanation: A shrinking, aging population leads governments to pronatalist policies like paid leave and child allowances. Closing the border would cut the immigration that is slowing the decline.

questions.stem: A country's population grows by 1.4% a year. At that rate, about how many years will it take to double?
questions.explanation: By the rule of 70, doubling time is about 70 divided by the growth rate in percent: 70 / 1.4 = 50 years. Seventy is the rule's numerator, not the answer.

questions.stem: People who flee persecution in their own country and cross an international border are
questions.explanation: Refugees have crossed a border because of a well-founded fear of persecution. People displaced inside their own country are internally displaced persons.

questions.stem: People forced from their homes by conflict or disaster who remain inside their own country are
questions.explanation: Internally displaced persons have not crossed an international border, so they fall outside the legal definition of a refugee and stay under their own government's protection.

questions.stem: Migrants who follow relatives who have already settled in a city are part of
questions.explanation: Chain migration follows links of family and community, as earlier migrants send information and help to those who follow. Step migration is a move made in stages.

questions.stem: Money that migrants working abroad send back to their families is called
questions.explanation: Remittances are a large source of income for many countries of emigration, paying for housing, schooling and small businesses at home.

questions.stem: A sex ratio at birth well above 105 boys per 100 girls most likely points to
options: more women than men emigrating each year
a strong cultural preference for sons
questions.explanation: About 105 boys per 100 girls is the natural ratio at birth. A much higher ratio suggests sex-selective abortion driven by son preference. Life expectancy affects older ages, not births.

questions.stem: The spread of teams from 2005 to 2012 best illustrates
questions.explanation: The sport jumped from the largest cities to the next largest, skipping the small places between them. Spread down the urban hierarchy is hierarchical diffusion.

questions.stem: The spread of amateur leagues from 2012 to 2020 adds which kind of diffusion?
questions.explanation: Leagues appeared first in the towns nearest a team city and then in the towns next to those, spreading through nearby places, which is contagious diffusion.

questions.stem: Which development would most likely have sped up the spread of the sport after 2012?
options: A fall in the share of people living in cities
Streaming of games online and on television
Laws banning sports leagues in small towns
Mountain ranges between the largest cities
questions.explanation: Broadcast and online media let people far from a team city see the game, a form of time-space compression that speeds diffusion. The other options would slow it.

questions.stem: Carl Sauer's idea of the cultural landscape refers to
options: the physical landscape before people arrived
a region defined by a single religion
a natural landscape as people have changed it
the paintings and music a culture produces
a map of where a group's languages are spoken
questions.explanation: Sauer defined the cultural landscape as the natural area shaped by a culture: its fields, buildings, roads and sacred sites. The landscape before people is the natural landscape.

questions.stem: Buddhism began in
questions.explanation: Buddhism arose in what is now northern India and Nepal, then spread to East and Southeast Asia, where most Buddhists live today.

questions.stem: A visitor who finds a local custom strange but tries to learn what it means to the people who practice it is showing
questions.explanation: Cultural relativism seeks to understand a culture on its own terms. Ethnocentrism, its opposite, judges other cultures by the standards of one's own.

questions.stem: An immigrant group that gives up its language and customs and adopts those of the host society has undergone
questions.explanation: Assimilation is the full absorption of a group into the host culture. Acculturation adopts some host traits while keeping much of the group's own.

questions.stem: Folk culture differs from popular culture in that folk culture
options: belongs to small groups and changes slowly
is much the same in many countries
spreads quickly through mass media and the internet
is produced mainly by large companies
is found mostly in large cities
questions.explanation: Folk culture is traditional, practiced by small and often rural groups, and passed on by word of mouth. The other options describe popular culture.

questions.stem: Compared with universalizing religions, ethnic religions tend to
options: seek converts in all parts of the world
trace back to a single founder known by name
be tied closely to their hearth's landscape
spread mainly down the urban hierarchy
questions.explanation: Ethnic religions are bound to one people and place, with holy rivers, mountains and cycles of local seasons. Universalizing religions seek converts everywhere and usually have a known founder.

questions.stem: Country V's shape is best described as
questions.explanation: An elongated state is long and narrow, which makes it hard to connect its far ends to the capital. A compact state is roughly round.

questions.stem: The northern region's elected assembly, which runs its own schools and police, is an example of
questions.explanation: Devolution transfers power from the central government to regional governments, often in response to ethnic or linguistic differences.

questions.stem: Which feature of Country V most likely acts as a centrifugal force?
options: Weak transport links to the north
The shared language of the plain
questions.explanation: A region with a distinct culture that is hard to reach from the capital is less tied to the state, which can feed separatism. The central capital and the railways are centripetal.

questions.stem: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a coastal state's exclusive economic zone reaches
questions.explanation: The exclusive economic zone gives a state rights to fish and seabed resources out to 200 nautical miles. Territorial waters end at 12 nautical miles.

questions.stem: Sovereignty means that a state
options: is home to only one nation
has final authority over its own territory
is formally recognized by every other state
questions.explanation: Sovereignty is a state's right to govern its territory without outside interference. Many sovereign states are multinational or federal.

questions.stem: After a census, a fixed number of legislative seats is shared out again among states by population. This is
questions.explanation: Reapportionment decides how many seats each state gets. Redistricting then redraws the district lines within a state.

questions.stem: The line where a former wall divided a city, still visible in the street pattern though no longer a border, is
questions.explanation: A relic boundary has stopped functioning as a border but can still be seen in the cultural landscape.

questions.stem: A state's claim to land across its border where people of its own ethnicity live is
questions.explanation: Irredentism seeks to bring an ethnic group living in a neighboring state, and the land it lives on, into the claiming state.

questions.stem: A region caught between stronger outside powers and divided within by ethnic or religious rivalries is
questions.explanation: In a shatterbelt, internal divisions and the rivalry of outside powers combine to produce repeated conflict.

questions.stem: Farming in which country is most likely mainly subsistence?
questions.explanation: Country G has most workers in farming, tiny farms, almost no tractors and sells only 22% of its output, so most food is eaten by the families who grow it.

questions.stem: Country K's enormous farms, few tractors per farm and nearly all output sold most likely reflect
options: intensive rice farming in flooded paddies
questions.explanation: Farms of thousands of hectares with little machinery and commercial sales point to extensive livestock ranching on land too dry for crops.

questions.stem: As Country H develops, its share of workers in farming will most likely
options: rise as more grassland is plowed for new crops
stay the same because land is limited
fall as workers move to industry and services
questions.explanation: Mechanization and larger farms need fewer workers, and growing industries and services draw people to cities, as Countries F and J show.

questions.stem: The Second Agricultural Revolution, linked to the Industrial Revolution, brought
options: the very first domestication of plants and animals
seed drills, crop rotation and new fertilizers
questions.explanation: From the 1700s new tools, rotations, fertilizers and later machinery raised yields and freed labor for factories. High-yield seeds came with the Green Revolution in the 1900s.

questions.stem: Crops whose genes have been altered in a laboratory, for example to resist pests, are
questions.explanation: Genetic modification changes a plant's DNA directly. Organic farming forbids such crops.

questions.stem: Large tropical estates that grow one cash crop for export, often owned by foreign firms, are
questions.explanation: Plantations grow crops such as bananas, sugarcane or oil palm for distant markets, a pattern dating from colonial rule.

questions.stem: Paddy rice farming in the densely populated river deltas of Asia is an example of
questions.explanation: Intensive agriculture puts much labor into small areas of land to get high yields, which suits crowded deltas where land is scarce.

questions.stem: An urban area where few stores sell fresh, healthy food is
questions.explanation: Food deserts are common in low-income neighborhoods with few supermarkets, where residents rely on convenience stores and fast food.

questions.stem: Fair trade certification aims mainly to
options: lower prices for shoppers in rich countries
give small farmers stable and fair prices
questions.explanation: Fair trade links farmers in poorer countries with buyers who agree to pay a minimum price and a premium, shortening an unequal commodity chain.

questions.stem: The city described best fits which model?
questions.explanation: A colonial plaza and CBD, an elite spine, middle-class rings improved over time and peripheral squatter settlements are the parts of the Griffin-Ford Latin American city model.

questions.stem: In that model, the wide avenue lined with offices and upscale housing is called
questions.explanation: The spine extends the CBD outward and is flanked by the elite residential sector. The disamenity sector holds the poorest housing, often on hazardous land.

questions.stem: The self-built settlements on the city's edge are most likely a result of
options: the flight of the rich to the suburbs
questions.explanation: Migrants arrive faster than formal housing and services can be built, so they build their own homes on land no one else wants, such as steep or flood-prone sites.

questions.stem: Hoyt's sector model holds that
options: land use is the same in every direction
cities grow in wedges along transport routes
cities grow in rings around one center
cities grow around several separate business centers
every city has a colonial port zone
questions.explanation: Hoyt saw high-rent, industrial and low-rent sectors extending outward along railways, roads and rivers. Rings around one center are Burgess's model.

questions.stem: The multiple nuclei model of Harris and Ullman differs from earlier models in
options: dividing the city into wedges along railways
questions.explanation: Harris and Ullman argued that cities grow around several nodes, such as a port, a university or an airport, each drawing related land uses.

questions.stem: In central place theory, the greatest distance people will travel to buy a good or service is its
questions.explanation: The range sets how far a market area can reach; the threshold is the minimum number of customers. Goods bought often have short ranges.

questions.stem: The practice of refusing home loans in certain neighborhoods, often by race, is
questions.explanation: Redlining marked neighborhoods as too risky for lending, which starved them of investment. Blockbusting played on racial fears to get owners to sell cheaply.

questions.stem: A city with more than 10 million people is
questions.explanation: A megacity is defined by its population. A megalopolis is a chain of metropolitan areas that have grown together.

questions.stem: Pavement and buildings that make a city warmer than the countryside around it create
questions.explanation: Dark surfaces absorb heat and buildings release it at night, so cities stay warmer, especially where trees are few.

questions.stem: Which country is most likely the least developed?
questions.explanation: Country M has the shortest lives, the least schooling and the most workers in agriculture, the profile of a least developed country.

questions.stem: Country P's figures show that
options: high development can coexist with gender inequality
schooling has no link to life expectancy
low life expectancy always comes with few women in parliament
Country P is less developed than Country M
farming countries have the most women in parliament
questions.explanation: Country P has long lives, much schooling and few farm workers, yet the lowest share of women in parliament, 9%. Country R, less developed, has 34%.

questions.stem: Which measure would best capture the gap shown for Country P?
questions.explanation: The Gender Inequality Index includes women's share of seats in parliament, so it would show Country P's gap. The HDI does not measure differences between women and men.

questions.stem: Dependency theory argues that many poorer countries stay poor mainly because
options: they have not yet reached Rostow's take-off stage
trade and colonial ties favor rich countries
questions.explanation: Dependency theorists hold that colonial history and unequal trade lock poorer countries into exporting raw materials to richer ones. Climate-based explanations are environmental determinism.

questions.stem: In world-systems theory, a fast-industrializing exporter with a mix of core and peripheral activities is part of the
questions.explanation: The semi-periphery both is exploited by the core and exploits the periphery, and countries can move into or out of it.

questions.stem: Software firms clustering in one region to share skilled workers, suppliers and ideas is
questions.explanation: Agglomeration gives firms that cluster lower costs and better access to labor and know-how. Deglomeration is the move away from a crowded cluster.

questions.stem: Foreign-owned factories in northern Mexico that assemble imported parts for export are
questions.explanation: Maquiladoras grew after rules allowed duty-free import of parts for assembly and re-export, mainly to the United States.

questions.stem: Flexible, just-in-time production in small batches, with work spread among many suppliers, is a feature of
questions.explanation: Fordism meant mass production of standard goods on assembly lines. Post-Fordist production adapts quickly to demand and outsources much of the work.

questions.stem: Tourism designed to protect natural areas and benefit local people is
questions.explanation: Ecotourism aims to earn income from nature while conserving it, giving local communities a reason to protect forests and wildlife.

questions.stem: Map 2 most likely uses a projection that preserves
questions.explanation: Map 2 keeps Greenland and Africa in correct proportion, so it is an equal-area projection, and it gives up shape to do so, which is why Africa looks stretched.

questions.stem: A student says Map 1 shows that Greenland is larger than Africa. The best response is that Map 1
options: is confirmed by the shapes on Map 3
greatly enlarges land far from the equator
draws Africa at a smaller scale on purpose
shows Greenland as it was in the past
is a reference map, so its areas are exact
questions.explanation: Map 1 is a Mercator-type projection, which stretches area more and more toward the poles. Africa is about 14 times the area of Greenland.

questions.stem: Map 3 is best described as
options: an azimuthal projection centered on a pole
a compromise projection that spreads distortion
a conformal projection made for navigation
an equal-area projection made for density maps
a cartogram sized by each country's population
questions.explanation: A compromise projection such as the Robinson keeps no property exactly but keeps all of them close for most of the world, which suits general reference world maps.

questions.stem: To show where farms of one crop are concentrated, with each dot standing for 100 farms, a cartographer would use
questions.explanation: A dot density map places one dot for a set number of features, so clusters show where they are concentrated. A choropleth shades whole areas by a rate instead.

questions.stem: Lines that join points of equal elevation or equal rainfall are the mark of
questions.explanation: An isoline map draws lines through points of equal value, such as contour lines of elevation or isohyets of rainfall.

questions.stem: A world map that redraws each country at a size set by its population is
questions.explanation: A cartogram distorts the size of each unit to show a value such as population. A choropleth keeps true boundaries and shades them instead.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the relative location of a town?
options: It is built on a terrace above a river
It has a population of about 40,000
It lies 20 km north of a major port
It sits at 41 degrees north, 12 degrees east
Its average July temperature is 24 C
questions.explanation: Relative location places somewhere in relation to other places. Latitude and longitude give absolute location, and the river terrace describes the town's site.

questions.stem: The physical features of the land on which a city is built, such as a hilltop or a harbor, are its
questions.explanation: Site is the physical character of the place itself. Situation is its location relative to other places, such as being on a trade route.

questions.stem: Regions such as the Bible Belt or the Midwest, whose borders differ from person to person, are
questions.explanation: A perceptual (vernacular) region exists in people's minds, so its boundaries vary by who is asked. Functional and nodal regions are the same idea, organized around a center.

questions.stem: Layering maps of roads, flood zones and existing schools to choose a site for a new school is a use of
questions.explanation: A GIS stores data in layers and lets the user overlay and query them, which is what site selection needs. GPS only fixes a position.

questions.stem: The discredited idea that climate shapes the abilities and behavior of whole societies is
questions.explanation: Environmental determinism claimed that the physical environment causes human traits. Geographers rejected it, partly because it was used to justify colonial rule.

questions.stem: Clearing forest from steep slopes to make new farmland most directly increases the risk of
options: lower water tables near the coast
questions.explanation: Tree roots and leaf litter hold soil on slopes. Without them, rain washes soil away and saturated slopes slide more easily.

questions.stem: About what share of City K's migrants came from within 50 km?
questions.explanation: 18,400 / 30,500 = 0.603, about 60%. Adding the 51 to 200 km row too gives about 84%.

questions.stem: The pattern for migrants from within the country best illustrates
questions.explanation: The number of migrants falls steadily as distance from City K rises, which is distance decay.

questions.stem: Ravenstein would predict that City K draws long-distance migrants mainly because it
options: has the most farmland around it
is close to the national border
has the oldest population in the country
is a large center of trade and industry
has a cooler climate than nearby towns
questions.explanation: Ravenstein observed that migrants who travel long distances usually head for great centers of commerce and industry, where jobs are most plentiful.

questions.stem: A family moves from a village to a market town and, years later, from the town to the capital. This is
questions.explanation: Step migration reaches a final destination through a series of smaller moves, often up the urban hierarchy.

questions.stem: A migrant heading for the capital who settles in a city along the way because she finds work there was drawn by
questions.explanation: An intervening opportunity is a pull factor met on the way that ends the journey early. An intervening obstacle is a barrier, such as a border or a mountain range.

questions.stem: Workers allowed to live in a country for a set period to fill labor shortages are
questions.explanation: Guest worker programs admit foreign workers on temporary permits, usually for farm, construction or factory work.

questions.stem: Ester Boserup argued that population growth
options: always ends in famine and war
has no effect on how land is farmed
makes farmers abandon their land for the cities
pushes farmers to adopt more intensive methods
questions.explanation: Boserup turned Malthus around: pressure from more people leads farmers to work land more intensively, with shorter fallow, irrigation and more labor, so output rises.

questions.stem: Neo-Malthusians differ from Malthus mainly in adding concern about
options: the arithmetic growth of the food supply
questions.explanation: Neo-Malthusians argue that growth strains not only food but water, energy and ecosystems. The arithmetic growth of food was Malthus's own idea.

questions.stem: Most of the world's people live
options: in the interiors of large deserts
at high elevations far away from the coasts and rivers
in lowlands with mild climates and fresh water
questions.explanation: People cluster where farming is easiest: river valleys, coastal plains and other lowlands with water and moderate climates, above all in East and South Asia.

questions.stem: The sharp drop in death rates in stage 2 of the demographic transition is mainly due to
options: falling birth rates as people move to cities
better food supply, sanitation and medicine
questions.explanation: Stage 2 begins when food, clean water and basic medicine lower death rates while birth rates stay high, so the population grows quickly.

questions.stem: A country's fertility falls to replacement level, yet its population keeps growing for decades. This is mainly because
options: many young adults are entering childbearing age
death rates rise sharply as the population grows older
questions.explanation: Population momentum: a large young generation born when fertility was high is now having children, so births stay above deaths even at about 2.1 children per woman.

questions.stem: Within most less developed countries today, the largest internal migration flow is
options: from the capital to small towns
questions.explanation: Rural-to-urban migration, driven by jobs and services in cities, is the main internal flow in most less developed countries and drives their rapid urbanization.

questions.stem: The landscape described is most closely tied to which religion?
questions.explanation: Ritual bathing in a sacred river, cremation on its banks and shrines to many gods are features of Hindu sacred landscapes.

questions.stem: The festival crowds described are an example of
questions.explanation: A pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred place for religious reasons, and its numbers swell at festivals.

questions.stem: The tent camps and extra trains show that a religious event can
options: end the diffusion of a religion abroad
lower the town's population for good
change national borders at a global scale
turn an ethnic religion into a universalizing one
change land use and services at a local scale
questions.explanation: For the festival weeks the town needs temporary housing, health care and transport, a local-scale effect of religion on land use.

questions.stem: After independence, a government renames streets and cities that had colonial names. This is an example of
options: the creation of a lingua franca
questions.explanation: Toponyms are place names. New states often replace colonial names to express national identity in the landscape.

questions.stem: A language that began as a pidgin and became the first language of a community is
questions.explanation: A pidgin is a simplified contact language with no native speakers. When children grow up speaking it, it develops into a full creole.

questions.stem: Basque, which is not related to any other living language, is
questions.explanation: A language isolate has no known relatives in any language family. Basque is still spoken in northern Spain and southwestern France.

questions.stem: Sikhism's hearth is
options: the Punjab region of South Asia
questions.explanation: Sikhism began in the Punjab, now divided between India and Pakistan, around 1500, and most Sikhs still live there.

questions.stem: Children of immigrants who speak the host language at school and work but keep their parents' religion and holidays show
questions.explanation: Acculturation is adopting some traits of the host culture while keeping core traits of one's own. Full assimilation would mean giving up the religion and holidays too.

questions.stem: A music style that began in poor urban neighborhoods and later spread to major labels and big cities shows
questions.explanation: Reverse hierarchical diffusion moves from people or places of lower status upward. Ordinary hierarchical diffusion starts at the top.

questions.stem: Global media that lead teenagers in many countries to dress alike contribute to
questions.explanation: Cultural convergence is the growing similarity of cultures as they come into contact, here through global media and brands.

questions.stem: Spanish, French and Italian are all
questions.explanation: The Romance branch of the Indo-European family grew out of the Latin spoken across the Roman Empire.

questions.stem: The belief that spirits live in natural features such as rivers, rocks and trees is
questions.explanation: Animism sees spirits in the natural world and is common in ethnic religions. Monotheism is belief in one god.

questions.stem: Border 2 is best classified as
questions.explanation: Border 2 was imposed by outside powers without regard to the people living there, and it follows a line of longitude, so it is both superimposed and geometric.

questions.stem: Border 3 is best classified as
questions.explanation: A consequent (ethnographic) boundary is drawn to fit cultural differences such as language. It is also subsequent, since the area was settled first.

questions.stem: Border 2 is most likely to cause which problem?
options: Disputes over a shifting river channel
Arguments over which peak is highest
A landlocked state losing access to the sea
A divided people crossing it to reach pastures
questions.explanation: A border that splits the seasonal pastures of one herding people cuts across their way of life, so herders cross it and states clash over them.

questions.stem: A state with no coastline, which must rely on its neighbors for access to ports, is
questions.explanation: A landlocked state has no sea access of its own, so trade agreements and transit routes through neighbors matter greatly.

questions.stem: A state that completely surrounds another state is
questions.explanation: A perforated state has a hole in it formed by another state, as South Africa surrounds Lesotho.

questions.stem: A state made up of many islands or of separated pieces of territory is
questions.explanation: A fragmented state's territory is split by water or by other states, which makes it harder to govern and connect.

questions.stem: A state in which most power is held by the central government is
questions.explanation: A unitary state governs from the center, and any regional bodies have only the powers the center gives them.

questions.stem: The principle that a people should be free to choose its own government is
questions.explanation: Self-determination underpinned the breakup of empires and decolonization after the world wars.

questions.stem: A district drawn so that a racial or ethnic minority makes up most of its voters is
options: a packed district for the majority
questions.explanation: Majority-minority districts are drawn to give a minority group the chance to elect a representative of its choice.

questions.stem: Spreading one party's voters thinly across many districts, so that they are outvoted in each, is
questions.explanation: Cracking dilutes a party's voting strength by splitting its supporters. Packing concentrates them in a few districts.

questions.stem: Joining a supranational union most directly requires a state to
options: merge with its neighbors into one state
adopt the language of the largest member
give up some control over its own policies
give up its seat at the United Nations
questions.explanation: Members pool sovereignty in areas such as trade rules, so some decisions are made at the union level instead of nationally.

questions.stem: Which would most likely act as a centripetal force?
questions.explanation: A shared language helps bind a state's people together. The other options can pull a state apart.

questions.stem: The stepped fields described are
options: long lots running back from a river
terraces that make flat land on slopes
fallow plots left to regrow forest
questions.explanation: Terracing cuts slopes into level steps that hold water and soil, allowing wet rice on steep land.

questions.stem: The village's settlement pattern is best described as
questions.explanation: The houses stand close together at the foot of the slope, a clustered pattern that leaves the slopes for fields.

questions.stem: The water buffalo in the landscape are most likely used mainly as
options: a source of wool for sale
pack animals for long trade journeys
draft animals for plowing wet fields
questions.explanation: In intensive rice farming water buffalo pull plows through flooded fields; the landscape shows hand labor and small plots, not commercial livestock.

questions.stem: Herding animals across dry lands with no permanent home is
questions.explanation: Pastoral nomads move with their herds in search of water and grazing, mainly in dry regions of Africa and Asia.

questions.stem: Growing grapes, olives and citrus where summers are dry and winters are mild is
questions.explanation: Mediterranean agriculture is found around the Mediterranean Sea and in similar climates such as California and central Chile.

questions.stem: The Green Revolution did least to raise yields of
options: millet and cassava in sub-Saharan Africa
wheat in the Punjab of India and Pakistan
rice in the irrigated plains of Southeast Asia
questions.explanation: The new varieties were bred for wheat and rice grown with irrigation and fertilizer. Africa's rain-fed staples such as millet, sorghum and cassava received little early research, and few farmers could afford the inputs.

questions.stem: The area around a city from which fresh milk can be delivered before it spoils is
questions.explanation: The milkshed is the zone that supplies a city's milk. Refrigeration has made milksheds far larger than they once were.

questions.stem: Overgrazing and drought turning dry grasslands into desert is called
questions.explanation: Desertification is the spread of desert-like conditions, often at the edges of deserts such as the Sahel. Salinization is salt build-up from irrigation.

questions.stem: Planting different crops in a field from season to season to keep the soil healthy is
questions.explanation: Rotating crops, for example legumes after grain, restores nutrients and breaks pest cycles. Monocropping grows one crop year after year.

questions.stem: Agribusiness refers to
options: farming run as a large, linked commercial system
farming carried out by a nomadic group
small family plots that feed only the farm household
questions.explanation: Agribusiness joins farming with seed, chemical, processing, transport and retail firms, often under one company or tight contracts.

questions.stem: Property lines that follow natural features such as streams, trees and large rocks are
questions.explanation: The metes and bounds system describes land by landmarks and distances, which gives irregular field shapes.

questions.stem: When shifting cultivators return to old plots before the forest has fully regrown, the main result is
questions.explanation: Shifting cultivation depends on a long fallow to rebuild soil. As population grows and fallow periods shorten, soils wear out.

questions.stem: Which statement is best supported by the data?
options: Tract 4 is the most densely settled
Older homes are found mostly in the outer tracts
Transit use rises as distance from the CBD rises
Density falls as distance from the CBD rises
All four tracts have similar density
questions.explanation: Density drops from 14,200 to 380 people per square km between Tracts 1 and 4, while transit use falls and the share of new homes rises.

questions.stem: How many more people per square km live in Tract 2 than in Tract 3?
questions.explanation: 7,800 - 2,100 = 5,700. Comparing Tract 1 with Tract 3 gives 12,100, and Tract 2 with Tract 4 gives 7,420.

questions.stem: Tract 4's figures are most consistent with
options: an old ethnic enclave near the CBD
a gentrifying inner-city district near the CBD
questions.explanation: Tract 4 is far from the CBD, sparsely settled, mostly built after 2000 and almost without transit riders: the profile of suburban sprawl.

questions.stem: Cities that serve as command centers of the global economy, home to major banks and corporate headquarters, are
questions.explanation: World cities link national economies to global finance and trade. Not every primate city is a world city.

questions.stem: In McGee's model of the Southeast Asian city, the focus of the city is
options: a market zone of street traders
questions.explanation: McGee found no single formal CBD; the city centers on the old colonial port zone, with commercial and government districts around it.

questions.stem: Informal settlements are best described as
options: housing built without legal title or permits
suburbs built by large private developers on farmland
questions.explanation: Residents of informal settlements build on land they do not own, often without water, sewers or secure tenure.

questions.stem: Clearing old inner-city housing to make way for highways and new buildings, as many cities did in the mid-1900s, is
questions.explanation: Urban renewal used public power to clear areas judged blighted, often displacing poor and minority residents.

questions.stem: Local laws that set which land uses are allowed in each part of a city are
questions.explanation: Zoning separates residential, commercial and industrial uses and can set density and building height.

questions.stem: Movement of people from cities to rural areas and small towns is
questions.explanation: Counterurbanization moves people out of the metropolitan area altogether, often as remote work and retirement free them from city jobs.

questions.stem: Smart growth policies aim mainly to
options: limit sprawl with compact, mixed-use growth
spread new housing across farmland at the urban edge
move factories to the city center
separate homes from shops and offices
questions.explanation: Smart growth steers new building toward existing areas with transit, protecting open land on the urban fringe.

questions.stem: The gravity model predicts that interaction between two cities grows with
options: the number of borders between them
questions.explanation: Interaction is proportional to the product of the populations divided by the distance between them, often squared.

questions.stem: Cleaning up abandoned, possibly polluted industrial land so that it can be reused is
questions.explanation: Brownfield redevelopment reuses land inside the city, unlike greenfield development on new land at the edge.

questions.stem: The district described is best identified as
questions.explanation: Special economic zones and export processing zones offer foreign firms lower taxes and duty-free inputs to attract export manufacturing.

questions.stem: The district's workforce most directly reflects
options: a return of retirees to the coast
transhumance between the coast and inland
questions.explanation: Young women moved from inland farming provinces to take factory jobs, the internal migration that comes with export manufacturing.

questions.stem: Which is a likely long-term criticism of the development model described?
options: Reliance on foreign firms that may leave
A shortage of workers moving to the coast
Rising farm employment in the district
questions.explanation: Firms drawn by tax breaks and low wages can move again when costs rise, and profits often leave the country, so growth may not last.

questions.stem: Under Weber's model, a soft drink bottler, whose product gains weight from local water, is best located
questions.explanation: A bulk-gaining industry locates near its customers, because water can be added locally and shipping the heavier finished product is costly.

questions.stem: A common criticism of Rostow's model is that it
options: treats farming as the goal of development
assumes every country follows Europe's path
pays too much attention to colonialism
questions.explanation: Rostow based his stages on Western experience and gave little weight to colonial history and unequal trade, which dependency and world-systems theorists stress.

questions.stem: Street vending and other work that is untaxed and not regulated by the government make up
questions.explanation: The informal sector is large in many less developed countries and is missed by official employment and income figures.

questions.stem: Research, data analysis and other knowledge-based services are often classed as
questions.explanation: The quaternary sector handles information and knowledge; it is a subdivision of the broad service (tertiary) economy.

questions.stem: A country that exports goods it can make at a lower opportunity cost than its trading partners is using
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage holds that both partners gain when each specializes in what it gives up least to produce.

questions.stem: An agreement among neighboring countries to remove tariffs on trade with one another creates
